subject: city billboards
title: What If a City Banned All Outdoor Ads? Sao Paulo Did in 2007

scenes.text: What if a city of 11 million banned every outdoor ad? Sao Paulo did in 2007.
The Clean City Law passed in September 2006 by a vote of 45 to 1. It took effect on January 1, 2007. Businesses had 90 days to comply.
About 15,000 billboards came down, plus towering metal panels and oversized shop signs. Fines ran up to 4,500 dollars a day.
Advertisers had spent over 100 million dollars on outdoor ads the year before. Critics warned of 20,000 lost jobs.
Then the city saw itself: old Art Deco facades, favelas the billboards had screened, immigrants living inside factories.
In surveys, more than 70 percent of residents backed the ban. Ads now creep back only in controlled spaces. The skyline stayed clear.

description:
What if a city banned every billboard? Sao Paulo's Clean City Law passed in September 2006 by 45 votes to 1 and took effect on 1 January 2007, removing about 15,000 billboards and thousands of oversized signs from a city of 11 million.
Advertisers had spent over 100 million dollars on outdoor ads in 2006, yet surveys found more than 70 percent of residents approved; the bare walls exposed old facades, favelas and workers living inside factories.
What should we run through next?

first_comment: Shops responded by painting their whole facades in bold colours to stand out without signs. Would you want your city to ban billboards?
